issue.body:

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 10 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1392 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​47 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1345 |
| Prod | 40 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1428 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​94 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1334 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## What this does, in plain terms

A chat with an agent only moves forward. If it went down a wrong path three messages ago, you can't take that back — you either keep arguing with a session whose context is already poisoned, or you throw it away and start over.

This adds the ability to **rewind a session back to an earlier message**: the agent forgets everything after that point, on its side and ours, and you carry on from there as if the detour never happened.

**This PR ships no button.** It is the engine only; the affordance that calls it is a separate PR. So nothing changes visually yet.

### Before → After (once the UI PR lands)

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agent misunderstood 3 messages back | Keep arguing, or abandon the session and lose all context | Revert to that message, re-ask properly |
| A bad tool result derailed the run | It stays in context forever, colouring every later answer | Truncate it away, continue clean |
| Recovering from a wrong turn | Hand-copy what you want into a fresh chat | The session itself steps back |

**It never touches your files.** Rewinding the conversation does not revert code on disk. Only chat history moves.

## Why a "step back a few messages" needs 1,300 lines

Because it is a destructive, irreversible operation on durable history, across two providers that behave differently, that must stay correct across crashes. Most of this PR is the safety, not the rewind. The four things that would have gone wrong:

1. **"The provider said OK" is not "we have the history."** Codex's revert reply deliberately returns an empty list plus a bookmark. Committing on the acknowledgment alone wrote a journal claiming to be the truncated conversation while holding only part of it. Acknowledgment and verified hydration are now distinct.
2. **A half-finished rewind could permanently block sending.** That is not a safe failure — it is a broken session that looks recoverable. An interrupted attempt now restores the original cursor and permits sending again.
3. **Some histories are too big to rewind — discoverable only *after* the destructive step.** 600 tiny turns pass the host's 10,000-item gate but blow the 1,024-row hydration budget. It now refuses up front with `history-limit` and leaves the session usable. Please don't later "simplify" this preflight as redundant with the item gate; the interaction is invisible if you read the two caps separately.
4. **A just-sent message couldn't be resolved to its provider target,** because accepted user messages kept Orca-side ids. Aliases now resolve to provider identities.

Old sessions from an older provider version can't do this at all, so they're refused cleanly and the UI can grey the option out rather than let you click it and fail.

## Interface contract for the UI PR

Nine refusal reason codes, final: `unsupported`, `history-not-paginated`, `busy`, `stale-epoch`, `invalid-target`, `history-limit`, `provider-refused`, `proof-mismatch`, `outcome-unknown`.

`outcome-unknown` means the revert may or may not have completed and sending is blocked until it resolves. It must never be surfaced as a clean failure.

---

## Technical detail

Adds backend-only `agentSession.rewind` using the existing mutation envelope, `itemId`, and fingerprinted `expectedEpoch`. The selected item is the first discarded: Codex discards its whole turn, while Claude resumes the same session at the preceding retained UUID. Accepted user-message aliases resolve to provider identities. Provider session IDs stay unchanged and workspace files are never reverted.

Rewind serializes with sends and refuses active, unresolved, concurrent, or stale work. Journal epochs commit only after exact Claude target proof or complete Codex hydration matching the preflight retained item identities. Provider acknowledgment alone cannot commit an epoch. Recovery retries bounded read-only reconciliation without repeating an ambiguous revert, and a crash after journal publication settles the existing epoch.

Codex performs bounded provider preflight **before** mutation, then verifies both paginated history indexes again afterward. This gate is necessary even with the host item limit: 600 tiny retained turns plus 600 item rows pass the host's 10,000-item gate but exceed the combined 1,024-row hydration budget. Discovering that only after revert would permanently block the session; it now refuses up front with `history-limit`. Provider reads are capped at 100 pages per index and 2 MiB combined, and the complete provider-derived prefix is saved before mutation so recovery also covers older turns missing from the local journal. Legacy-history threads remain unsupported.

Claude consumes explicit ancestor authorization on its first proof attempt, including failures. Exact proof checkpoints the resumable provider head and success record atomically before later acquisition work. An interrupted unproven attempt restores the original cursor with ordinary exact proof, without reusing ancestor authorization, and permits sending again.

Durable refusal reasons stay open bounded strings; RPC emission retains these nine codes: `unsupported`, `history-not-paginated`, `busy`, `stale-epoch`, `invalid-target`, `history-limit`, `provider-refused`, `proof-mismatch`, `outcome-unknown`. Unknown roles preserve visible content with a system-role fallback. No renderer, locale, journal-kind, or stream-opcode change.

Validation: same-model safety review is clean and opening/ending readiness findings are resolved. On the merged branch, 520 tests passed across 70 suites; one new main adoption-replay test fails identically at line 188 on a clean detached `origin/main` checkout (`314506003a`) and was left unchanged. Changed-file lint and pre-commit checks passed. Merge `60f9c021ba` has two verified parents, and all resolution files match the committed versions. Central typecheck and live Electron/provider QA remain coordinator-owned.

**Automated Reviews**: Continuous reviews of the pull requests including incremental commits.

**Insights into your code**:  Ask any questions on your codebase within the pull request 

**Chat about your code** : Chat with the bot around your code. The more you chat, the smarter it gets.

**Issue Validation**:  Validates the PR against the linked issues and identifies other related issues

## Status: ready for review

Backend only — the user-facing affordance is a separate PR.

### Plan review
Reviewed before any code was written. Verdict **APPROVE WITH AMENDMENTS**; all five applied. Two policy calls were accepted with conditions:

- **Codex legacy-history threads are refused, not migrated.** Migrating would silently rewrite a thread's stored history mode as a side effect of a destructive verb. The condition was that refusal be detectable *before* the user acts, so an unsupported marker is exposed through the session capability surface and the UI can disable rather than fail late.
- **Claude multi-turn rewind uses an explicit cursor resume** rather than iterating `resumeDropsTurn`, which validates only one dropped prompt. Iterating would multiply destructive steps and partial-failure states. What makes it safe is ordering: the journal commits only after the proof observes the leaf equals the requested target.

### Code review loop — four real recovery defects found and fixed
This is where the value was. Same-model subagent review plus `readiness-checklist` at both ends proved four defects, none of which tests or lint would have caught:

1. **Unverified hydration committed as a completed epoch.** The provider's revert reply deliberately returns empty turns plus backwards cursors, so an acknowledgment proves acceptance, not possession of the retained history. Committing on that basis writes a journal claiming to be the truncated history while holding whatever subset arrived. Now: acknowledgment and verified hydration are distinguished, and a partial hydration never commits.
2. **Prepared interruptions permanently blocked sends.** Not a safe failure — a destroyed session that looks recoverable. Now checkpointed, and an unproven attempt is restored through normal resume proof before unblocking, so the proof is re-earned rather than assumed.
3. **A limit discoverable only *after* the destructive step.** Many small retained turns individually pass the per-item gate but exceed the provider's combined hydration limit — which only surfaced post-revert. Now a bounded preflight refuses up front (`history-limit`) and the original session stays usable. Worth preserving: this interaction is invisible if you read the caps individually, so please don't fold the preflight back into the item gate as "redundant".
4. **Accepted user messages retained Orca journal IDs**, so rewind could not resolve their provider targets and could mismatch a Claude prefix. The host now resolves accepted submission aliases for both targets and retained prefixes, and persists the complete provider prefix before mutation so crash recovery works even when older provider turns were absent locally.

Both readiness runs ended clean for PR scope. 520 tests across 70 suites pass on the merged tree.

### Verification
- Central typecheck run by the coordinator: **exit 0, zero errors**, post-merge.
- Main merged with a **verified two-parent** merge commit (a failing pre-commit hook destroys `MERGE_HEAD` and silently produces a single-parent commit, so this was checked explicitly).
- One `adoption-replay` test fails on the merged tree. This was **proven pre-existing on main**: the unchanged test fails identically, at the same line and assertion, on a clean detached `origin/main` checkout. It was reproduced independently by two different lanes. No unrelated test was edited to go green.

### Interface contract for the dependent UI PR
Nine refusal reason codes, confirmed stable and final across all four fixes:

`unsupported`, `history-not-paginated`, `busy`, `stale-epoch`, `invalid-target`, `history-limit`, `provider-refused`, `proof-mismatch`, `outcome-unknown`

`outcome-unknown` must be surfaced as genuine uncertainty — the revert may or may not have completed and sending is blocked until resolved — never as a clean failure.

### Scope notes
- Claude's dropped branch remains in the on-disk transcript by design; reverting files is out of scope.
- No renderer changes, no forking, no new journal item kind.
- Durable refusal reasons are open bounded strings so an older build can still parse its own recovery record after a rollback; the closed typed set is applied at the RPC boundary.

### Process deviations, stated plainly
- **No Electron validation.** This PR has no user-visible surface, so screenshots would show nothing. Visual evidence belongs to the UI PR that consumes this. Producing a screenshot here would be evidence-shaped rather than evidence.
- **Severity counsel unavailable.** `readiness-checklist`'s counsel step needs nested agent seats; nested worker depth is 1 in this install. Recorded as unavailable rather than reported as a verdict.

## ELI5 — what this PR actually does

**The problem in one sentence.** A chat with an agent only moves forward. If it goes down a wrong path three messages ago, there is no way to take that back — you either live with the bad context poisoning everything after it, or you throw the whole session away and start over.

**What this adds.** The machinery to rewind a session back to an earlier message: the agent forgets everything after that point, on both its side and ours, and you can carry on from there as if the detour never happened.

**Important: this PR ships no button.** It is the engine only. The affordance you click is a separate PR that builds on this one. So the honest user-facing before/after today is *nothing visible changes*. The before/after below is what the pair of PRs delivers once the UI lands.

### Before → After (once the UI PR lands)

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Agent misunderstands 3 messages back | Keep arguing with it, or abandon the session and lose all context | Revert to that message and re-ask it properly |
| A bad tool result derails the run | It stays in context forever, influencing every later answer | Truncate it away and continue clean |
| Recovering from a wrong turn | Copy what you want to keep into a brand-new chat by hand | The session itself steps back |

### Why the diff is large for "step back a few messages"

Because it is a **destructive, irreversible operation on durable history**, and it has to be safe across two different agent providers that behave differently, plus crashes. Most of this PR is the safety, not the rewind:

- Both providers keep their own copy of the conversation. Rewinding means changing *their* history and *ours* and keeping the two agreeing — including when the app is killed halfway through.
- One provider's revert reply deliberately hands back an empty list plus a bookmark, so "the provider said OK" is not the same as "we actually have the history". Treating those as the same wrote a journal that *claimed* to be the truncated conversation while holding only part of it. Fixed.
- If we half-finish a rewind and get interrupted, the session must not end up permanently unable to send. That is not a safe failure — it is a broken session that looks recoverable. Fixed.
- Some histories are too big to rewind safely, and that was only discoverable *after* the destructive step had already happened. Now it refuses up front and leaves your session untouched.
- Old sessions from an older provider version can't do this at all, so they are refused cleanly and the UI can grey the option out rather than letting you click it and fail.

### What it deliberately does not do

- **It does not touch your files.** Rewinding the conversation does not revert code on disk. Only the chat history moves.
- It does not delete the agent's own on-disk transcript; it stops using the part after your chosen point.
- It does not fork. Forking a session from a point is a separate PR.
